seasons.review_body: Warrior Nun debuted on Netflix in July 2020, adapted from Ben Dunn's comic by showrunner Simon Barry and filmed largely in Spain. The premise - a paralysed young woman resurrected by a holy artefact that bonds to her spine, forcing her into a secret Catholic warrior order - sounds maximalist, and in Season 1 the show sometimes struggles to balance its mythology-building with its character work. Critics landed at 69 percent from 36 reviews, with reservations centring on heavy-handed setup and world-construction that occasionally stalls the pace. The audience found the same material considerably more compelling - 94 percent on Rotten Tomatoes with over 2,500 ratings - pointing to the show's genuine strength: Alba Baptista's performance as Ava Silva, the fight choreography filmed in Spanish architecture, and a sincerity about its genre premise that the algorithm-era rarely allows. Season 1 is the rougher half of the show's run, but it plants the foundations the second season would build on.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Warrior Nun S1E1: "Psalm 46:5" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

**Ava** says her whole life she dreamed about being dead. The hour takes that ugly little wish and hands it back as a problem. She died, she walks, and nobody in the room has a clean explanation. Around her, religious threat language and emergency procedure collide. A nun warns that the Devil can wear a pleasing face. The sisters talk about shrapnel that must come out before it kills. The pilot's sharpest idea is simple: resurrection arrives as evidence. Someone has to explain the body.

That choice keeps the premiere from floating into instant prophecy. Ava's return has wonder in it, but the episode treats wonder as unstable matter. It has mass. It leaves marks. It gets people killed, or at least makes everyone afraid that it will. The result is a pilot with a clean hook and a crowded first movement, strong enough to carry its mythology even when the script tries to unpack too much at once.

## A Death Wish Gets Its Invoice

The opening works because it refuses to make Ava's return neat. Her first defining contradiction is neither heroism nor belief. She wants to understand why she is alive again, and her method is physical: test what is possible, ask what is happening, keep pressing until the dream gives way to consequence. That gives the pilot a useful engine. The supernatural becomes personal before it becomes institutional.

Ava's blunt reaction once she understands this is no dream lands cleanly: "This is hardcore real life." It is funny because it is underwritten. No grand speech. No chosen-one pose. No instant acceptance. Just a girl realizing that death has spat her back into a world that now expects an explanation from her body.

The episode is sharpest when it lets Ava be confused in practical terms. She does not begin by solving the mythology. She begins by discovering that the impossible has rules, and that other people may know more about those rules than she does. That is the right starting point for this story. Ava has lived under the control of other people, other rooms, other caretakers. Resurrection should feel like freedom, but the pilot keeps making it feel like another system preparing to claim her.

That is why the physical comedy and body horror matter. Ava is not simply told she has changed. She has to learn it through movement, pain, surprise, and bad decisions. The body that once trapped her now refuses to behave according to any known rule. The hour plants its central question cleanly: if Ava died and is walking, what brought her back, and what price is attached to that second chance?

The danger is that the pilot occasionally pushes Ava toward mystery-box function before her emotional situation has fully settled. Her confusion is compelling because it is immediate. When the hour lets the institutions talk around her for too long, it risks turning her into the object of the plot rather than the person at its center. The stronger scenes remember that Ava is not an abstract miracle. She is a dead girl who woke up hungry for answers and control.

## Protocol Before Prayer

The pilot's opening injury sequence is built on pressure, and the pressure is mostly procedural. The sisters address "Divinium shrapnel" and warn that it must be removed before it kills. That phrasing matters. The show gives its supernatural vocabulary a material edge: shrapnel, removal, explosives, fatal risk. The threat has weight because it is lodged inside a body.

That choice gives the hour texture. The nun's warning that the Devil may present a pleasing visage frames the spiritual suspicion around what is happening, but the scene around Shannon does not drift into sermon. It stays busy. Short exchanges stack up. People give orders. A wound has a cause. A clock is running.

The downside shows early. The dialogue density makes the pilot feel as if it is trying to smuggle a handbook through a crisis scene. The terms arrive fast, and some of the urgency has to share space with explanation. The hour survives because the explanations are tied to action, but the first movement is cramped. It wants dread, lore, team dynamics, and medical panic in the same breath. That is a heavy load for an opening sequence.

Still, the pressure gives the world a useful shape. The Order is introduced through work rather than pageantry. These women have doctrine, but they also have tasks. They cut, extract, carry, report, decide. That makes the religious framing sharper than it would be if the show leaned only on icons and ominous Latin. The sacred object has logistics. The wound has a procedure. Faith does not cancel triage.

That balance is the pilot's best world-building choice. It makes the church setting feel operational, not just decorative. The episode can talk about demons and holy purpose because it has already shown hands working on a dying body. The supernatural language earns more trust when it shares the frame with blood, metal, and panic.

## Mary Makes Panic Behave

**Mary** gives the injury plot its spine. Her stated job is immediate: handle Shannon's condition, keep the team moving, follow the steps that might preserve a life. The interesting tension is that Mary later reports Shannon's wounding with the bluntness of an account, while the episode keeps stressing the mission's necessity and the fatal risk. She talks like someone filing the facts because facts are the only things that can still be controlled.

That makes her useful in a pilot crowded with impossible events. **Shannon** can say she will buy time, but Mary is the one who turns that time into procedure. The episode needs that contrast. Shannon's sacrifice beat gives the hour urgency. Mary's account gives it structure.

The writing makes Mary's contradiction productive. She is calm because the scene requires someone to make panic behave. That is where the show finds a firmer rhythm: injury, report, risk, recovery. Each piece pushes the next. When Mary explains that Shannon was critically wounded by Divinium mixed with explosives, the pilot turns a chaotic opening into a chain of cause and consequence.

Mary also helps define the emotional rules of the Order. The sisters are not interchangeable action figures. The mission asks for obedience, but the episode keeps showing how personal loss breaks through that discipline. Mary knows the language of duty. She also knows Shannon was a person, not only a bearer of an object or a fallen soldier in a holy chain of command. That friction gives her presence bite.

The pilot could use more room for that grief. It moves quickly from Shannon's injury to the Halo crisis to Ava's awakening, and the speed makes sense for a premiere trying to hook an audience. Even so, Mary's hardness works because it suggests an emotional backlog. She has no time to collapse. The next decision is already waiting.

## The Halo Refuses to Be a Blessing

**Father Vincent** enters the hour through questions. He wants answers and trustworthy handling of the Halo situation, and he pushes for information because the facts do not add up. That is the right function for him in this episode. He acts as a pressure point, forcing the room to say what it knows and admit what it does not.

The Halo is smartest here as a question. Has it ever brought someone back before? Will removing it kill Ava? Why was there an impression that Shannon had no family or friends? These open loops are not decorative. They keep the pilot from turning Ava's revival into a simple empowerment beat. The object that may have saved her may also kill her if handled wrongly.

That is a strong hook because it complicates the chosen-object idea without overselling the complication. Ava's resurrection could have been played as instant destiny. Instead, the episode frames it as a custody problem, a medical risk, and a theological disturbance. The Halo works because nobody is allowed to admire it for long. Every possible blessing comes with a procedure attached.

Vincent's role also keeps the show from flattening the church into a single mood. Suspicion, belief, caution, and damage all sit in the same institution. That gives the pilot more room to maneuver later. The Order can be protective and possessive. It can be a refuge and a machine. Ava's body forces those tensions into the open.

The episode is careful to make the Halo feel powerful before it feels understandable. That matters. A pilot can drown its central object in rules too soon. Here, the rules arrive as fear. People know enough to be alarmed. They do not know enough to be safe. That is a better dramatic position than certainty, especially for a season built around a reluctant bearer and an institution trying to catch up with its own sacred machinery.

## The Verdict

"Psalm 46:5" is a solid, slightly overloaded pilot with a clean central argument: coming back to life does not free Ava, it makes her the evidence everyone wants to control. The hour is best when it stays concrete: a dead girl walking, shrapnel that must be removed, Shannon buying time, Mary turning crisis into protocol, Father Vincent demanding answers. It weakens when early exposition crowds the injury sequence and makes the mythology feel packed rather than discovered.

Still, the episode earns its season slot. It plants the Halo, Ava's impossible return, Shannon's fatal risk, and Mary's procedural hardness without pretending any of them are solved. The mythology is heavy, but the body count and bodily stakes keep it grounded. Ava's second chance arrives with witnesses, handlers, questions, and danger. That is enough for a sturdy launch. BollyAI's score: 7.3/10.

Reviewers consistently cited the bisexual romance arc, the science-fiction integration with religious mythology, and Baptista's grown performance as the season's defining improvements.

pull_quotes.text: Excellent action-adventure TV, with complex and nuanced women leads, and a bisexual love story anchoring the whole thing in place.
Season 2 is where things really kick into a new gear, fully blending science fiction and religion in a way I was not expecting.
A shining beacon of excellent romance, world-building, and commentary on our world that doesn't lag in its sophomore season.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 of Warrior Nun arrived in November 2022 and critics responded to a markedly more confident show - 100 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 11 reviews, a result that reflected both genuine improvement and the self-selecting nature of a smaller critical pool covering a cancelled series' final run. The show's central romance between Ava and Sister Beatrice (Kristina Tonteri-Young) developed into what multiple reviewers described as the season's emotional spine. Simon Barry's writing blended the series' science-fiction mythology more fluidly with its religious architecture, and the result felt like the show the first season was trying to become. Netflix cancelled Warrior Nun weeks after the season landed, citing viewing metrics - a decision that generated one of the more sustained fan campaigns in recent streaming history. Season 2 stands as the definitive version of the show: cleaner, bolder, and operating at a level the first season only periodically reached.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 fully integrates the science-fiction and religious mythology threads Season 1 kept separate, and the central romance moves from subtext to the load-bearing emotional structure.
